# Quantitative Magnesium Evaporation Loss During LPBF of AlSi10Mg

## 1. Measured Fractional/Relative Mg Loss: Powder vs. As-Built Composition

Direct quantitative measurements of Mg loss between powder feedstock and as-built LPBF parts are surprisingly scarce for AlSi10Mg specifically, though several closely related studies provide strong constraints.

**AlSi10Mg and AlSi7Mg0.6 (Low-Mg Al-Si alloys):** Multiple studies of AlSi10Mg powder recycling have found that the main alloying element composition—including Mg—does not change significantly during LPBF. Weiss et al. (2022) performed ICP-AES analysis of AlSi10Mg powder over 10 recycling cycles on an SLM280HL (up to 400 W, 60 µm layer thickness, Ar atmosphere) and reported "no major change" in the main constituents of the powder, including Mg (pqac-00000022). Maamoun et al. (2018) measured AlSi10Mg powder composition by EDS and found fresh powder contained 0.37 wt% Mg while recycled powder contained 0.34 wt% Mg—a difference of only ~0.03 wt%, within EDS uncertainty (pqac-00000026). Smolina et al. (2022) performed XRF analysis on both AlSi7Mg0.6 powder and LPBF-fabricated bulk specimens across five reuse cycles. The powder Mg content ranged from 0.61–0.72 wt%, while the as-built LPBF specimens measured 0.715–0.735 wt% Mg. The authors concluded that "the magnesium content in the alloy did not change significantly in the case of both the powder and solid samples" (pqac-00000023). These results suggest that for Al-Si alloys with ≤0.7 wt% Mg processed under typical LPBF conditions, the **net measurable Mg loss is negligible to very small (<5%)** within the resolution of EDS/XRF techniques.

**Al-Zn-Mg alloys (Higher-Mg systems):** The most quantitative direct powder-to-part comparison comes from Babu et al. (2020), who measured chemical composition by ICP-AES for three custom Al-Zn-Mg alloys processed by LPBF at 95 W and 175 mm/s. The Mg content decreased from 2.3 → 2.1 wt% (8.7% relative loss) for Al-10Zn-2Mg, from 3.34 → 2.79 wt% (16.5% relative loss) for Al-14Zn-3Mg, and from 4.40 → 3.28 wt% (25.5% relative loss) for Al-18Zn-4Mg (pqac-00000032). The latter alloy also exhibited cracking attributed to the appreciable evaporative loss of both Zn and Mg (pqac-00000020).

**Al-Mg-Sc (Scalmalloy®):** Electromagnetic levitation (EML) experiments by Bärtl et al. (2022) represent an upper-bound reference case. When Scalmalloy® (~4.9 wt% Mg) was superheated to T_L + 540 K for approximately 45 seconds in EML processing, the Langmuir-based prediction and experimental measurement showed **100% Mg loss**—all 9.056 × 10⁻³ g of Mg evaporated completely (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000017). The total alloy mass loss was 3.75% actual (3.01% predicted), dominated by Mg evaporation. While this is not a direct LPBF experiment, it confirms that Mg has the highest evaporation propensity among alloying elements in Al-Mg alloys.

The following table compiles the available quantitative data:

| Study (reference) | Alloy system | Measurement technique | Powder Mg (wt%) | As-built Mg (wt%) | Absolute Mg loss (wt%) | Relative Mg loss (%) | Process parameters (power, speed) | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Maamoun et al. 2018 | AlSi10Mg | EDS | 0.37 (fresh), 0.34 (recycled) | NR | NR | NR | 370 W, 1300 mm/s | Powder-only comparison; no bulk as-built Mg reported directly. Recycled-vs-fresh powder difference = -0.03 wt% Mg (~8% lower in recycled powder), but this is not powder-to-part loss. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) |
| Weiss et al. 2022 | AlSi10Mg | ICP-AES | NR | NR | ~0 | ~0 | SLM280HL, up to 400 W; 60 µm layer | Authors report no major change in main alloying elements during recycling; quantitative Mg values not given in retrieved text. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022) |
| Smolina et al. 2022 | AlSi7Mg0.6 | XRF | 0.61-0.72 | 0.715-0.735 | ~0 to +0.105 | ~0 to +17 | NR in retrieved text | Within XRF scatter, Mg remained essentially unchanged; some bulk values are slightly higher than powder, so no measurable net Mg depletion was resolved. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000023) |
| Tradowsky et al. 2016 | AlSi10Mg | Powder chemistry table | 0.30 | NR | NR | NR | Concept Laser M2; up to 400 W | Powder composition reported; retrieved text did not include bulk/as-built Mg measurement. Useful baseline for nominal AlSi10Mg feedstock Mg level. (pqac-00000024) |
| Babu et al. 2020 | Al-10Zn-2Mg | ICP-AES | 2.30 | 2.10 | 0.20 | 8.7 | 95 W, 175 mm/s | Direct measured powder-to-post-LPBF Mg loss. Same study also reported Zn loss. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032) |
| Babu et al. 2020 | Al-14Zn-3Mg | ICP-AES | 3.34 | 2.79 | 0.55 | 16.5 | 95 W, 175 mm/s | Direct measured powder-to-post-LPBF Mg loss. Loss larger than in Al-10Zn-2Mg. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032) |
| Babu et al. 2020 | Al-18Zn-4Mg | ICP-AES | 4.40 | 3.28 | 1.12 | 25.5 | 95 W, 175 mm/s | Direct measured powder-to-post-LPBF Mg loss; highest Mg loss of the three alloys, with cracking also attributed to appreciable Zn/Mg vaporization. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032) |
| Bärtl et al. 2022 | Scalmalloy® (Al-Mg-Sc-Mn-Zr) | EML levitation + Langmuir-based evaporation analysis | NR as wt%; Table 5 gives Mg initial mass 9.056×10^-3 g | 0 (post-EML Mg mass) | 100% of Mg present | 100 | Not LPBF; EML at TL+540 K superheat for ~45 s | Extreme reference case, not directly LPBF bulk composition. Shows Mg is the fastest-evaporating species and can be fully removed under sustained superheat. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000034) |
| Zhao 2024 | AlMgScZr (DED) | EDX | NR | NR | Qualitative only | Qualitative only | DED; examples include 550-900 W, 450-550 mm/min | EDX showed lower Mg in remelted vs un-remelted layers; higher surface Mg can be artifactually elevated by Mg-rich soot. No extractable bulk wt% loss reported in retrieved text. (pqac-00000028) |


*Table: This table compiles the quantitative and semi-quantitative magnesium loss evidence retrieved from the literature for Al-Si-Mg, Al-Mg-Sc, and related aluminum alloys processed by LPBF/SLM/DED. It highlights which studies provide true powder-to-part Mg comparisons and which only provide powder baselines, qualitative evidence, or non-LPBF bounding cases.*

## 2. Process Parameter and Atmosphere Dependence

**Energy density:** Vaporization of alloying elements intensifies with increasing volumetric energy density (VED). Shi et al. (2024), in a comprehensive review, noted that higher energy density inputs more heat to the melt pool, leading to higher peak temperatures and more intensified vaporization, with scanning speed having a greater impact on metal vaporization than laser power alone (pqac-00000031). This is consistent with the Langmuir model, in which evaporation flux increases exponentially with temperature through the vapor pressure term.

**Langmuir evaporation model:** The theoretical framework for predicting element loss in LPBF is well-established. Mukherjee and DebRoy (2016) showed that the vaporization flux J_i of alloying element i can be estimated from the Langmuir equation: J_i = λP_i / √(2πM_iT), where P_i is the vapor pressure, M_i is the molecular weight, T is the melt pool temperature, and λ is a condensation factor (pqac-00000004). Bärtl et al. (2022) extended this with an activity-based formulation: (1/M_i)(dm_i/dt) = a_i·P_{v,i}·A_s / √(2πM_iR_GT), where a_i = γ_i·c_i is the activity (activity coefficient × concentration) (pqac-00000016). Critically, a shielding factor α = 1/(1 + K·P_G^n) accounts for the suppression of evaporation by the inert gas atmosphere: with K = 0.012 and n = 1.0 for metallic elements in Ar, at typical LPBF chamber pressure (~750 mbar), α ≈ 1.11 × 10⁻³, meaning the Ar atmosphere reduces evaporation by approximately three orders of magnitude compared to vacuum (pqac-00000016). The vapor pressure P_{v,i} follows Alcock's four-term equation and increases strongly with temperature. For Mg, the boiling point of 1091°C is far below typical melt pool peak temperatures (>2000°C near the laser spot), making it the most volatile species in Al-Si-Mg alloys (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000018).

**Atmosphere effects:** The Ar shielding gas plays a dual role: (i) providing an inert environment and (ii) dramatically suppressing evaporation kinetics. Helium provides weaker shielding, with evaporation rates approximately 2× faster than in Ar for elements with molar mass >20 g/mol (pqac-00000016). Higher gas flow rates can remove evaporation fume more efficiently from the melt zone (pqac-00000030), but the primary suppression comes from gas pressure.

## 3. Concentration Dependence of Fractional Mg Loss

The Langmuir model predicts that the evaporation mass flux of element i is proportional to its activity a_i = γ_i·x_i, where x_i is the mole fraction in the melt and γ_i is the activity coefficient (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000004). For an ideal dilute solution (γ_i ≈ constant), the absolute mass evaporation rate scales linearly with concentration, which implies that the **fractional (relative) loss should be approximately independent of initial concentration** when the melt pool thermal history is held constant.

However, the experimental data from Babu et al. (2020) show that fractional Mg loss increases with initial Mg content: 8.7% at 2.3 wt%, 16.5% at 3.34 wt%, and 25.5% at 4.40 wt% Mg (pqac-00000032). This apparent increase likely reflects that the higher-Mg alloys also had substantially higher Zn content (10.8–19.2 wt%), and the combined evaporative cooling effects, different melt pool dynamics, and non-ideal thermodynamic behavior all contribute. Additionally, in the Bärtl et al. (2022) EML experiments, the very high Mg content (~4.9 wt%) in Scalmalloy enabled complete Mg depletion, illustrating that at high initial concentrations, the Mg activity is sufficient to drive very rapid evaporation (pqac-00000034).

For AlSi10Mg with only 0.20–0.45 wt% Mg (specification range), or even lower at 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg, the Mg mole fraction is very small (~0.05–0.15 at.%), and the absolute evaporation driving force is correspondingly weak. The Langmuir framework suggests that if the relative loss at 0.3–0.4 wt% Mg is already below the detection limits of EDS/XRF (i.e., ≲5%), then at 0.05–0.07 wt% the relative loss should be comparable or less. The key insight is that the thermal history of the melt pool is primarily dictated by the Al-Si matrix (not the trace Mg), so reducing Mg content does not significantly change the evaporative conditions, but it does reduce the total mass of Mg available per melt pool, making the absolute loss smaller.

## 4. Predicted Mg Content for 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg Feedstock

Based on the combined evidence, the following predictions can be made:

| Scenario | Assumed relative Mg loss (%) | Powder Mg (wt%) | Predicted as-built Mg (wt%) | Basis/rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Conservative (minimal loss) | 0-5 | 0.05-0.07 | 0.047-0.070 | Near-zero measurable composition change reported for AlSi10Mg powder recycling and AlSi7Mg0.6 powder/bulk comparisons; consistent with low Mg volatility impact under stable Ar LPBF conditions (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Moderate loss | 5-15 | 0.05-0.07 | 0.043-0.067 | Extrapolated from LPBF Al-Zn-Mg data showing Mg losses of ~9-17% at 2.3-3.34 wt% Mg, combined with Langmuir/activity scaling for dilute Mg in Al alloys (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000016) |
| High loss (upper bound) | 15-25 | 0.05-0.07 | 0.038-0.060 | Upper-bound case representing hotter/aggressive conditions, higher effective superheat, or stronger vaporization; informed by highest measured LPBF Mg loss in Al-18Zn-4Mg and general energy-density trends (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000031) |
| Best estimate | 0-10 | 0.05-0.07 | 0.045-0.070 | Typical AlSi10Mg LPBF window (~200-400 W, 1000-1600 mm/s, Ar) likely closer to negligible-to-small Mg loss than high-Mg alloy behavior; practical expectation centered near ~0.05-0.065 wt% Mg (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000031) |


*Table: This table gives scenario-based predicted magnesium ranges for as-built LPBF parts starting from 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg powder. It is useful for estimating likely retained Mg under typical AlSi10Mg processing and for bounding uncertainty with literature-based loss assumptions.*

**Best estimate:** Under typical AlSi10Mg LPBF parameters (200–400 W, 1000–1600 mm/s, Ar atmosphere, ~30–60 µm layers), the expected Mg content in as-built parts from a 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg powder is approximately **0.045–0.070 wt% Mg**, corresponding to 0–10% relative loss. The central expectation is near-complete Mg retention, based on the following reasoning:

1. Studies on AlSi10Mg recycling (Weiss et al. 2022; Maamoun et al. 2018) and AlSi7Mg0.6 bulk/powder comparisons (Smolina et al. 2022) consistently report negligible measurable Mg composition change under optimized LPBF parameters (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000023).

2. The Langmuir model predicts that Ar atmosphere at ~750–1000 mbar reduces evaporation rates by ~1000× relative to vacuum, making the absolute Mg loss per melt pool pass very small (pqac-00000016).

3. At 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg, the Mg activity is 5–8× lower than in standard AlSi10Mg (0.3–0.4 wt%), further reducing the evaporative driving force (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000016).

Quantitative magnesium evaporation loss during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) of AlSi10Mg.

Context: Mg has a boiling point (1091 C) below the melting point of Si (1414 C) and far below LPBF melt-pool peak temperatures, so selective Mg vaporization is expected. Our feedstock powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg (below the nominal 0.20-0.45 wt% AlSi10Mg specification), and we want to predict the Mg content in the as-built part.

Questions to answer with quantitative literature data:
1. What fractional/relative Mg loss (percent of initial Mg content, or absolute wt% drop) has been measured between AlSi10Mg powder and as-built LPBF parts? Cite specific studies with measured powder vs. as-built Mg wt% values and the measurement technique (ICP-OES, EDS, XRF, etc.).
2. How does Mg loss depend on process parameters (laser power, scan speed, volumetric energy density, hatch spacing) and machine atmosphere (Ar flow, chamber pressure)? Is there a model (e.g., Langmuir evaporation-based) that predicts element loss in LPBF, and what does it predict for Mg in Al alloys?
3. Does fractional Mg loss depend on the initial Mg concentration (i.e., is relative loss roughly constant so results from 0.3-0.4 wt% powders can be scaled to a 0.05-0.07 wt% powder)?
4. Based on the literature, what Mg wt% range should be expected in as-built parts if the powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg under typical AlSi10Mg LPBF parameters (roughly 200-400 W, 1000-1600 mm/s, Ar atmosphere)?

Provide numeric estimates with uncertainty and cite the primary sources.

This excerpt presents a **Langmuir equation-based model** for predicting elemental vaporization during laser additive manufacturing. The vaporization flux is calculated as: **Ji = λPi / √(2πMiT)** (equation 8), where Pi is vapor pressure, Mi is molecular weight, T is temperature, and λ accounts for condensation. The vaporized mass is: **Δmi = LAs·Ji / v** (equation 9), where L is track length, As is melt pool surface area, and v is scanning speed. Final composition after vaporization is: **Wf = (VρWi - Δmi) / (Vρ - ΣΔmi)** (equation 11), where Wi is initial weight percentage.

The model is demonstrated on multiple alloys (SS 316, Ti-6Al-4V, IN 625, etc.), with **Figure 4 showing composition changes in volatile elements** under "Parameter Set 3." However, **the excerpt does not provide specific quantitative data for Mg loss in AlSi10Mg**, measured powder vs. as-built Mg concentrations, or how loss varies with process parameters like laser power or scan speed.

# Summary

This excerpt describes an experimental methodology for studying powder reuse in LPBF (laser powder bed fusion) of AlSi7Mg0.6 alloy using a "continuous reuse" approach per ASTM F3456-22. Starting with 15 kg of virgin powder, samples were produced across multiple process cycles (S0–S4), with powder recycled and double-sieved between cycles. Final usable powder weight was 11 kg, with a part-to-powder ratio of approximately 1:10 depending on cycle number.

Powder and bulk samples were characterized for morphology (laser diffraction, SEM), flowability (GranuDrum), laser absorption (spectrophotometry at 900–1100 nm), and chemical composition via energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence (ED-XRF) with 3× repetition per series. Tensile dogbone specimens (100 mm length per ASTM E8/E8M-16) were machined from produced plates, and sample quality was evaluated using X-ray computed tomography (XCT).

**Note:** This excerpt does not contain the quantitative Mg loss data, process parameter dependencies, or predictive models requested in the question.

# Summary

The excerpt discusses numerical simulation approaches to studying vaporization in LPBF processes, particularly for magnesium alloys. Yi Luo's evaporation model found that "vaporization time of Mg, Al, and Zn was Mg < Zn < Al," showing magnesium vaporizes prior to other elements due to its lower vaporization temperature. Wei Kaiwen and J Jakumeit integrated "relationship formulas related to element burning loss and metal surface evaporation flux," establishing foundations for quantitative analysis. However, the excerpt notes limitations: models often "regarded metal vapor as an ideal gas and alloy materials as a single pure metal material," and "absorption, reflection and shielding of the laser as well as thermal radiation and emissivity of the materials are difficult to measure." Yu-Che Wu's simulations found that "melt track formed considering vaporization was narrow but deep, and the vaporization effect reduced the surface temperature." The excerpt addresses modeling approaches but does not provide specific measured Mg wt% loss data or quantitative predictions for the 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg powder case.

# Summary

The excerpt presents a Langmuir evaporation model (Eq. 4) for predicting element mass loss during thermal processing of metallic alloys. Key findings include:

**Evaporation Model**: Element evaporation rate depends on vapor pressure (Pv,i), activity coefficient (ai), surface area, and temperature. The shielding factor (a) accounts for inert gas atmosphere effects—for argon at 750 mbar, a ≈ 1.11 × 10⁻³.

**Specific Element Losses**: Mg in Scalmalloy evaporated quickly with 540 K superheat in 45 seconds; Mn showed moderate loss (7.9% total) but accelerated to >70% at 970 K superheat in Zicromal. Al showed 0.13-0.15% loss at 530-540 K superheat, increasing to 3.3% at 970 K.

**Predictions vs. Actual**: Table 5 data shows predicted mass losses agreed reasonably with experimental results, though predictions were slightly lower because cooling gas flow enhanced evaporation beyond model predictions.

The model is stated as "applicable to laser-melting or manufacturing process," suggesting potential transferability to LPBF, though specific AlSi10Mg LPBF data is not provided in this excerpt.

# Summary

The excerpt describes a comprehensive study of AlSi10Mg parts fabricated via SLM (selective laser melting) using recycled powder under defined process parameters (370 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 0.19 mm hatch spacing, 30 μm layer thickness). Powder characterization via particle size distribution (PSD), XRD, EDS, and XPS analysis showed fresh and recycled powders had nearly identical chemical composition with consistent standard deviations, and similar crystal sizes. XRD confirmed Al and Si phases with "absence of Mg2Si precipitates inside the powder composition." XPS detected magnesium aluminum oxide (MgAl2O5) surface films (2–4 nm thickness) on fresh powder. The study examined thermal post-processing effects (annealing at 200–300°C, SHT at 530°C/1h and 530°C/5h, and T6 heat treatment) but does **not provide specific quantitative Mg loss data** (wt% reduction from powder to as-built parts) or element loss models for LPBF conditions.
contexts.question:
Quantitative magnesium evaporation loss during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) of AlSi10Mg.

Context: Mg has a boiling point (1091 C) below the melting point of Si (1414 C) and far below LPBF melt-pool peak temperatures, so selective Mg vaporization is expected. Our feedstock powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg (below the nominal 0.20-0.45 wt% AlSi10Mg specification), and we want to predict the Mg content in the as-built part.

Questions to answer with quantitative literature data:
1. What fractional/relative Mg loss (percent of initial Mg content, or absolute wt% drop) has been measured between AlSi10Mg powder and as-built LPBF parts? Cite specific studies with measured powder vs. as-built Mg wt% values and the measurement technique (ICP-OES, EDS, XRF, etc.).
2. How does Mg loss depend on process parameters (laser power, scan speed, volumetric energy density, hatch spacing) and machine atmosphere (Ar flow, chamber pressure)? Is there a model (e.g., Langmuir evaporation-based) that predicts element loss in LPBF, and what does it predict for Mg in Al alloys?
3. Does fractional Mg loss depend on the initial Mg concentration (i.e., is relative loss roughly constant so results from 0.3-0.4 wt% powders can be scaled to a 0.05-0.07 wt% powder)?
4. Based on the literature, what Mg wt% range should be expected in as-built parts if the powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg under typical AlSi10Mg LPBF parameters (roughly 200-400 W, 1000-1600 mm/s, Ar atmosphere)?

Provide numeric estimates with uncertainty and cite the primary sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that Mg evaporation in aluminum alloys depends significantly on temperature (superheat). In Scalmalloy®, Mg evaporates rapidly with a superheat of 540 K over 45 seconds. The Langmuir evaporation model predicts element loss rates using vapor pressure, temperature, and a shielding factor accounting for inert gas atmosphere. Key predictive factors include activity coefficients, surface area, molar mass, and vapor pressure described by Alcock's equation. The study shows total mass loss predictions align well with experimental results. Process parameters like powder size distribution and volume energy density influence evaporation indirectly—smaller powder particles require lower power density/volume energy density. However, the excerpt does not explicitly detail direct relationships between specific LPBF parameters (laser power, scan speed, volumetric energy density) and Mg loss rates. The analysis indicates that lower-boiling point elements like Mg experience faster evaporation at higher superheats, and predictions could be improved using non-ideal solution models with accurate activity coefficients.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses evaporation in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of zinc metal using the Langmuir model. According to the theoretical analysis, evaporation flux of element i (Ji) depends on molten pool temperature (T), saturated vapor pressure (Pi0), and molar mass (Mi). The evaporation loss of alloying elements increases with increasing laser energy input because higher laser power causes increased temperature in the molten pool. The evaporation loss tendency ranks as Zn > Mg > Fe > Ti, indicating Mg has lower evaporation loss than Zn but higher than Fe and Ti. The Langmuir model shows that saturated vapor pressure increases with temperature, and evaporation flux increases with temperature. Additionally, compositional change is related to the original concentration of alloying elements, with lower concentrations tending to produce higher relative losses at similar evaporation rates. However, the excerpt focuses on pure Zn and does not specifically address aluminum alloys or scan speed parameters.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses how process parameters affect metal vaporization in LPBF, including Mg and Al elements. Higher energy density intensifies metal vaporization of Mg powder, while lower scanning speeds drive temperature diffusion in Al alloy molten pools, increasing surface instability. Research shows that as energy density increases, vaporization amounts increase proportionally, with greater laser penetration power and plume formation. Notably, scanning speed has a greater impact on metal vaporization than laser power alone. The general principle is that greater energy density inputs more heat, leading to higher metal powder temperatures and more intensified vaporization. # Quantitative Magnesium Evaporation Loss During LPBF of AlSi10Mg

## 1. Measured Fractional/Relative Mg Loss: Powder vs. As-Built Composition

Direct quantitative measurements of Mg loss between powder feedstock and as-built LPBF parts are surprisingly scarce for AlSi10Mg specifically, though several closely related studies provide strong constraints.

**AlSi10Mg and AlSi7Mg0.6 (Low-Mg Al-Si alloys):** Multiple studies of AlSi10Mg powder recycling have found that the main alloying element composition—including Mg—does not change significantly during LPBF. Weiss et al. (2022) performed ICP-AES analysis of AlSi10Mg powder over 10 recycling cycles on an SLM280HL (up to 400 W, 60 µm layer thickness, Ar atmosphere) and reported "no major change" in the main constituents of the powder, including Mg (weiss2022ontheinfluence pages 4-5). Maamoun et al. (2018) measured AlSi10Mg powder composition by EDS and found fresh powder contained 0.37 wt% Mg while recycled powder contained 0.34 wt% Mg—a difference of only ~0.03 wt%, within EDS uncertainty (maamoun2018thermalpostprocessingof pages 3-5). Smolina et al. (2022) performed XRF analysis on both AlSi7Mg0.6 powder and LPBF-fabricated bulk specimens across five reuse cycles. The powder Mg content ranged from 0.61–0.72 wt%, while the as-built LPBF specimens measured 0.715–0.735 wt% Mg. The authors concluded that "the magnesium content in the alloy did not change significantly in the case of both the powder and solid samples" (smolina2022influenceofthe pages 8-11). These results suggest that for Al-Si alloys with ≤0.7 wt% Mg processed under typical LPBF conditions, the **net measurable Mg loss is negligible to very small (<5%)** within the resolution of EDS/XRF techniques.

**Al-Zn-Mg alloys (Higher-Mg systems):** The most quantitative direct powder-to-part comparison comes from Babu et al. (2020), who measured chemical composition by ICP-AES for three custom Al-Zn-Mg alloys processed by LPBF at 95 W and 175 mm/s. The Mg content decreased from 2.3 → 2.1 wt% (8.7% relative loss) for Al-10Zn-2Mg, from 3.34 → 2.79 wt% (16.5% relative loss) for Al-14Zn-3Mg, and from 4.40 → 3.28 wt% (25.5% relative loss) for Al-18Zn-4Mg (babu2020laserpowderbed media 7a4d691d). The latter alloy also exhibited cracking attributed to the appreciable evaporative loss of both Zn and Mg (babu2020laserpowderbed pages 4-7).

**Al-Mg-Sc (Scalmalloy®):** Electromagnetic levitation (EML) experiments by Bärtl et al. (2022) represent an upper-bound reference case. When Scalmalloy® (~4.9 wt% Mg) was superheated to T_L + 540 K for approximately 45 seconds in EML processing, the Langmuir-based prediction and experimental measurement showed **100% Mg loss**—all 9.056 × 10⁻³ g of Mg evaporated completely (bartl2022influenceofsurface media 4e1d16d5, bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 10-10). The total alloy mass loss was 3.75% actual (3.01% predicted), dominated by Mg evaporation. While this is not a direct LPBF experiment, it confirms that Mg has the highest evaporation propensity among alloying elements in Al-Mg alloys.

The following table compiles the available quantitative data:

| Study (reference) | Alloy system | Measurement technique | Powder Mg (wt%) | As-built Mg (wt%) | Absolute Mg loss (wt%) | Relative Mg loss (%) | Process parameters (power, speed) | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Maamoun et al. 2018 | AlSi10Mg | EDS | 0.37 (fresh), 0.34 (recycled) | NR | NR | NR | 370 W, 1300 mm/s | Powder-only comparison; no bulk as-built Mg reported directly. Recycled-vs-fresh powder difference = -0.03 wt% Mg (~8% lower in recycled powder), but this is not powder-to-part loss. (maamoun2018thermalpostprocessingof pages 2-3, maamoun2018thermalpostprocessingof pages 3-5) |
| Weiss et al. 2022 | AlSi10Mg | ICP-AES | NR | NR | ~0 | ~0 | SLM280HL, up to 400 W; 60 µm layer | Authors report no major change in main alloying elements during recycling; quantitative Mg values not given in retrieved text. (weiss2022ontheinfluence pages 3-4, weiss2022ontheinfluence pages 4-5) |
| Smolina et al. 2022 | AlSi7Mg0.6 | XRF | 0.61-0.72 | 0.715-0.735 | ~0 to +0.105 | ~0 to +17 | NR in retrieved text | Within XRF scatter, Mg remained essentially unchanged; some bulk values are slightly higher than powder, so no measurable net Mg depletion was resolved. (smolina2022influenceofthe pages 4-6, smolina2022influenceofthe pages 8-11) |
| Tradowsky et al. 2016 | AlSi10Mg | Powder chemistry table | 0.30 | NR | NR | NR | Concept Laser M2; up to 400 W | Powder composition reported; retrieved text did not include bulk/as-built Mg measurement. ## 2. Process Parameter and Atmosphere Dependence

**Energy density:** Vaporization of alloying elements intensifies with increasing volumetric energy density (VED). Shi et al. (2024), in a comprehensive review, noted that higher energy density inputs more heat to the melt pool, leading to higher peak temperatures and more intensified vaporization, with scanning speed having a greater impact on metal vaporization than laser power alone (shi2024areviewof pages 17-21). This is consistent with the Langmuir model, in which evaporation flux increases exponentially with temperature through the vapor pressure term.

**Langmuir evaporation model:** The theoretical framework for predicting element loss in LPBF is well-established. Mukherjee and DebRoy (2016) showed that the vaporization flux J_i of alloying element i can be estimated from the Langmuir equation: J_i = λP_i / √(2πM_iT), where P_i is the vapor pressure, M_i is the molecular weight, T is the melt pool temperature, and λ is a condensation factor (mukherjee2016printabilityofalloys pages 4-6). Bärtl et al. (2022) extended this with an activity-based formulation: (1/M_i)(dm_i/dt) = a_i·P_{v,i}·A_s / √(2πM_iR_GT), where a_i = γ_i·c_i is the activity (activity coefficient × concentration) (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10). Critically, a shielding factor α = 1/(1 + K·P_G^n) accounts for the suppression of evaporation by the inert gas atmosphere: with K = 0.012 and n = 1.0 for metallic elements in Ar, at typical LPBF chamber pressure (~750 mbar), α ≈ 1.11 × 10⁻³, meaning the Ar atmosphere reduces evaporation by approximately three orders of magnitude compared to vacuum (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10). The vapor pressure P_{v,i} follows Alcock's four-term equation and increases strongly with temperature. For Mg, the boiling point of 1091°C is far below typical melt pool peak temperatures (>2000°C near the laser spot), making it the most volatile species in Al-Si-Mg alloys (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 5-7, bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 10-11).

**Atmosphere effects:** The Ar shielding gas plays a dual role: (i) providing an inert environment and (ii) dramatically suppressing evaporation kinetics. Helium provides weaker shielding, with evaporation rates approximately 2× faster than in Ar for elements with molar mass >20 g/mol (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10). Higher gas flow rates can remove evaporation fume more efficiently from the melt zone (qin2021influenceoflaser pages 7-10), but the primary suppression comes from gas pressure.

## 3. Concentration Dependence of Fractional Mg Loss

The Langmuir model predicts that the evaporation mass flux of element i is proportional to its activity a_i = γ_i·x_i, where x_i is the mole fraction in the melt and γ_i is the activity coefficient (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10, mukherjee2016printabilityofalloys pages 4-6). For an ideal dilute solution (γ_i ≈ constant), the absolute mass evaporation rate scales linearly with concentration, which implies that the **fractional (relative) loss should be approximately independent of initial concentration** when the melt pool thermal history is held constant.

However, the experimental data from Babu et al. (2020) show that fractional Mg loss increases with initial Mg content: 8.7% at 2.3 wt%, 16.5% at 3.34 wt%, and 25.5% at 4.40 wt% Mg (babu2020laserpowderbed media 7a4d691d). This apparent increase likely reflects that the higher-Mg alloys also had substantially higher Zn content (10.8–19.2 wt%), and the combined evaporative cooling effects, different melt pool dynamics, and non-ideal thermodynamic behavior all contribute. Additionally, in the Bärtl et al. (2022) EML experiments, the very high Mg content (~4.9 wt%) in Scalmalloy enabled complete Mg depletion, illustrating that at high initial concentrations, the Mg activity is sufficient to drive very rapid evaporation (bartl2022influenceofsurface media 4e1d16d5).

For AlSi10Mg with only 0.20–0.45 wt% Mg (specification range), or even lower at 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg, the Mg mole fraction is very small (~0.05–0.15 at.%), and the absolute evaporation driving force is correspondingly weak. The Langmuir framework suggests that if the relative loss at 0.3–0.4 wt% Mg is already below the detection limits of EDS/XRF (i.e., ≲5%), then at 0.05–0.07 wt% the relative loss should be comparable or less. The key insight is that the thermal history of the melt pool is primarily dictated by the Al-Si matrix (not the trace Mg), so reducing Mg content does not significantly change the evaporative conditions, but it does reduce the total mass of Mg available per melt pool, making the absolute loss smaller.

## 4. Predicted Mg Content for 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg Feedstock

Based on the combined evidence, the following predictions can be made:

| Scenario | Assumed relative Mg loss (%) | Powder Mg (wt%) | Predicted as-built Mg (wt%) | Basis/rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|

| Moderate loss | 5-15 | 0.05-0.07 | 0.043-0.067 | Extrapolated from LPBF Al-Zn-Mg data showing Mg losses of ~9-17% at 2.3-3.34 wt% Mg, combined with Langmuir/activity scaling for dilute Mg in Al alloys (babu2020laserpowderbed pages 4-7, babu2020laserpowderbed media 7a4d691d, mukherjee2016printabilityofalloys pages 4-6, bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10) |

*Table: This table gives scenario-based predicted magnesium ranges for as-built LPBF parts starting from 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg powder. It is useful for estimating likely retained Mg under typical AlSi10Mg processing and for bounding uncertainty with literature-based loss assumptions.*

**Best estimate:** Under typical AlSi10Mg LPBF parameters (200–400 W, 1000–1600 mm/s, Ar atmosphere, ~30–60 µm layers), the expected Mg content in as-built parts from a 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg powder is approximately **0.045–0.070 wt% Mg**, corresponding to 0–10% relative loss. The central expectation is near-complete Mg retention, based on the following reasoning:

1. Studies on AlSi10Mg recycling (Weiss et al. 2022; Maamoun et al. 2018) and AlSi7Mg0.6 bulk/powder comparisons (Smolina et al. 2022) consistently report negligible measurable Mg composition change under optimized LPBF parameters (weiss2022ontheinfluence pages 4-5, maamoun2018thermalpostprocessingof pages 3-5, smolina2022influenceofthe pages 8-11).

2. The Langmuir model predicts that Ar atmosphere at ~750–1000 mbar reduces evaporation rates by ~1000× relative to vacuum, making the absolute Mg loss per melt pool pass very small (bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10).

3. At 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg, the Mg activity is 5–8× lower than in standard AlSi10Mg (0.3–0.4 wt%), further reducing the evaporative driving force (mukherjee2016printabilityofalloys pages 4-6, bartl2022influenceofsurface pages 8-10).

4. The dominant Mg loss mechanism in practice may be surface oxide formation (MgAl₂O₄ spinel) on spatter particles rather than bulk melt pool evaporation, as demonstrated by Raza et al. (2021) who observed progressive Mg enrichment in oxide nodules on AlSi10Mg spatter particles (raza2021degradationofalsi10mg pages 4-6, raza2021degradationofalsi10mg pages 6-8).

**Uncertainties and caveats:** (i) Aggressive process parameters (very high VED, slow scan speeds, keyhole-mode melting) could significantly increase Mg loss. (ii) Multiple remelting passes or remelting strategies increase total Mg evaporation, as shown for DED of AlMgScZr where remelted layers had lower Mg than un-remelted layers (zhao2024directedenergydeposition pages 65-70). (iii) The EDS/XRF measurement uncertainty (~0.02–0.05 wt% for Mg at these low levels) limits the ability to resolve small changes, so ICP-OES on digested bulk samples would be the recommended measurement approach for detecting losses of 0.005–0.01 wt% Mg. (iv) The already-low Mg content of the powder (0.05–0.07 wt%) is well below the AlSi10Mg specification minimum (0.20 wt%), meaning that even without any evaporative loss, the Mg₂Si age-hardening response will be severely limited regardless.

**Summary:** For a 0.05–0.07 wt% Mg AlSi10Mg powder processed under standard LPBF conditions in Ar, the predicted as-built Mg content is approximately **0.045–0.070 wt%**, with the most likely outcome being near-complete retention of the already-low Mg content. Any losses are expected to be ≤0.01 wt% in absolute terms, which is at or below the typical analytical uncertainty of EDS and comparable to the detection limits even for ICP-OES at these concentrations.

info.query:
Quantitative magnesium evaporation loss during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / SLM) of AlSi10Mg.

Context: Mg has a boiling point (1091 C) below the melting point of Si (1414 C) and far below LPBF melt-pool peak temperatures, so selective Mg vaporization is expected. Our feedstock powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg (below the nominal 0.20-0.45 wt% AlSi10Mg specification), and we want to predict the Mg content in the as-built part.

Questions to answer with quantitative literature data:
1. What fractional/relative Mg loss (percent of initial Mg content, or absolute wt% drop) has been measured between AlSi10Mg powder and as-built LPBF parts? Cite specific studies with measured powder vs. as-built Mg wt% values and the measurement technique (ICP-OES, EDS, XRF, etc.).
2. How does Mg loss depend on process parameters (laser power, scan speed, volumetric energy density, hatch spacing) and machine atmosphere (Ar flow, chamber pressure)? Is there a model (e.g., Langmuir evaporation-based) that predicts element loss in LPBF, and what does it predict for Mg in Al alloys?
3. Does fractional Mg loss depend on the initial Mg concentration (i.e., is relative loss roughly constant so results from 0.3-0.4 wt% powders can be scaled to a 0.05-0.07 wt% powder)?
4. Based on the literature, what Mg wt% range should be expected in as-built parts if the powder contains 0.05-0.07 wt% Mg under typical AlSi10Mg LPBF parameters (roughly 200-400 W, 1000-1600 mm/s, Ar atmosphere)?

Provide numeric estimates with uncertainty and cite the primary sources.
